t.4.9.1: My elder brother, named Vālī, a destroyer of enemies, was always highly esteemed by our father, and so too was he by me in former days.
t.4.9.2: When our father had passed away, the ministers, saying "This is the eldest," made him, highly esteemed, lord of the monkeys in the kingdom.
t.4.9.3: While he ruled the great kingdom inherited from father and grandfather, I stood humbly bowed before him at all times, like a servant.
t.4.9.6: But my brother Vālī, who was fast asleep, heard that roar of terrible sound and could not bear it; then he rushed out with great speed.
t.4.9.4: There was a mighty one named Māyāvī, a son and the elder brother of Dundubhi. Long ago a great enmity arose between him and Vālin on account of a woman, and it became widely known.
t.4.9.5: At night, while the people were asleep, he came to the gate of Kiṣkindhā, roared in great fury, and challenged Vālin to battle.
t.4.9.7: But he, in his anger, rushed out to slay that foremost of asuras, though he was being held back by the women and by me, bowing humbly before him.
t.4.9.8: But that mighty one, shaking us all off, went forth; then I too, out of affection, set out together with Vālin.
t.4.9.9: But that asura, on seeing my brother and me standing at a distance, was seized with terror and then fled away in great haste.
t.4.9.10: As he fled in terror, the two of us went after him all the more swiftly, and the path was lit up then by the rising moon.
t.4.9.11: That asura rushed swiftly into a great cavern in the earth, hard to reach and covered over with grass, while we two, having arrived there, stood still.
t.4.9.12: Seeing that enemy enter the cave, Vālī, overcome by rage, his senses agitated, then spoke these words to me.
t.4.9.13: Sugrīva, stay here at the mouth of the cave, alert and watchful, while I enter in and slay the enemy in battle.
t.4.9.15: More than a full year passed after he had entered the cave, and all that time went by while I stood waiting at its entrance.
t.4.9.14: Having heard these words, I entreated him, O scorcher of foes; but he made me swear by his feet and then entered the cave.
t.4.9.16: But I, knowing him to be lost and seized with agitation out of affection, could not see my brother anywhere, and my mind feared that some evil had befallen him.
t.4.9.17: Then, after a long time, I saw red, frothing blood issuing forth from that cave, and I was deeply grieved.
t.4.9.18: The din of the roaring asuras reached my ears, and with it the cry of my elder brother, wailing as he was struck down in the battle.
t.4.9.19: But I, having concluded through reasoning from those signs that my brother had been slain, closed the mouth of the cave with a rock the size of a mountain, and, stricken with grief, offered the water-libation and came back to Kiṣkindhā, my friend.
t.4.9.20: Though I tried to conceal the truth, the ministers learned it through diligent effort. Then, after I had met with them, I was consecrated by them all assembled together.
t.4.9.21: O Rāghava, while I was ruling the kingdom justly, Vālī returned, having slain his enemy, that foremost of asuras.
t.4.9.22: But seeing me consecrated as king, his eyes reddened with anger, he bound the ministers from my side and spoke harsh words.
t.4.9.23: Though I was capable of restraining that wicked one, O Rāghava, my mind did not turn against him, held in check as it was by reverence for my brother.
t.4.9.24: Honoring that great-souled one, I saluted him as was proper, but no blessings were spoken by him with a contented heart.
